passage: Beta, when I was in Class 6, our maths teacher asked, "If two trains leave the station at the same time, which arrives first?" Everyone shouted answers. I sat still, chin in my hand, looking at the window, and Omkar poked me. "Hemant, say something!" I didn't. I was working it out. The teacher, Mr Bose, saw me and said, "Let him finish." He waited, ten seconds maybe, which felt very long. Then I said, "It depends on how fast and how far." He smiled. "The only right answer." I remember that wait more than the question. Omkar still says I looked asleep. I wasn't. I was thinking.

qa.q: What was Hemant looking at while he was quiet?
qa.a: He was looking at the window.

qa.q: How was Hemant feeling as he sat still with his chin in his hand, and how did Omkar read it?
qa.a: He was calm and absorbed, quietly working the answer out rather than bored. Omkar read the same stillness as sleepiness and poked him.

qa.q: What could a teacher do when a child is quiet after a question?
qa.a: Wait a few extra seconds, as Mr Bose did, so the child can finish thinking.

qa.q: How might Omkar have felt while Hemant stayed silent?
qa.a: Omkar poked him and told him to say something, so he was probably impatient or worried on his friend's behalf.

grounding: An elder recalls going quiet and looking away while working out an answer, and a teacher who waited a few extra seconds.

passage: It was almost the end of the exam, and the fan had stopped in the power cut. Mehak sat still, tapping her chin with the end of her pen and looking at the ceiling. The invigilator, Sonali, noticed the time and walked toward her desk, but then stopped a few steps away. The clock said four minutes left. Mehak's eyes moved as if reading the air. Then she leaned forward and wrote in a burst, three lines, before the bell. Sonali collected the papers and read Mehak's last answer quickly. It was the best one on the page. She said nothing but smiled.

qa.q: What did Mehak tap her chin with?
qa.a: She tapped her chin with the end of her pen.

qa.q: What did Mehak's stillness and looking at the ceiling suggest she was doing, and what else could it mean?
qa.a: It suggested she was thinking through her answer. It might also have meant she was stuck, but her burst of writing shows she was working it out.

qa.q: What could Sonali do when a student seems to pause during a test?
qa.a: Wait a moment before intervening, since silence often means thinking, and leave the student enough time to finish.

qa.q: How might Mehak feel when she writes her last lines just before the bell?
qa.a: She may feel a rush of relief or determination, having finished the answer she was working out under time pressure.

grounding: A child goes quiet and taps her chin while working out an answer, and an adult waits a few extra seconds under time pressure.

passage:
In the crowded Delhi metro, Chinmay Mama gave Sahil a riddle: "What has keys but can't open locks?"
Sahil went quiet. He looked at the window, then tapped his chin with one finger. The train rattled through two stations.
A lady beside them leaned in. "Should I tell him?"
Chinmay shook his head. "He's thinking. Give him time."
Sahil's lips moved silently. His eyes narrowed.
"A piano!" he burst out, as the doors opened at Rajiv Chowk.
Chinmay laughed. "Right! And you got it yourself."
Sahil grinned all the way to the exit.

qa.q: What riddle did Chinmay Mama give Sahil?
qa.a: "What has keys but can't open locks?"

qa.q: What does Sahil tapping his chin and looking out the window suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he was thinking hard and focused, not confused or bored.

qa.q: Why was it helpful that Chinmay waited instead of giving the answer?
qa.a: Waiting let Sahil finish his own thinking and feel proud when he got it. 😊

qa.q: How might the lady beside them see Sahil's silence at first?
qa.a: She probably thought he was stuck or needed help, not that he was thinking.

grounding: A child goes quiet and taps his chin while solving a riddle, and an adult waits to let him finish.

passage:
"Tanuja, what's the capital of Rajasthan?"
Tanuja looked at the ceiling and bit her lip.
"She doesn't know!" shouted Raju from the back.
"Wait," said Jagdish Sir. "Give her a few seconds."
Tanuja's eyes moved as if reading something invisible. "Um... it's... Jaipur."
"Correct," said Sir. "Raju, silence can mean thinking."
"But she took ages!"
"Ten seconds isn't ages. Sometimes the answer needs a moment to arrive."
Tanuja smiled. "I was trying to remember the map on the wall at home."
"Good strategy," Sir said. "Next question, Raju. Take your time too."

qa.q: What was the capital Tanuja named?
qa.a: Jaipur.

qa.q: What was Tanuja thinking about when she looked at the ceiling?
qa.a: She was thinking and trying to remember the map at home, feeling focused, not confused.

qa.q: How did Jagdish Sir support Tanuja?
qa.a: He stopped Raju's interruption and gave her a few extra seconds, letting her finish her thought.

qa.q: How might Raju see silence differently after Sir's explanation?
qa.a: Raju might learn that silence often means someone is thinking, not that they don't know.

grounding: A teacher gives a child time to think, showing that silence often means thinking.

passage:
At the inter-school quiz, the question was: "Which planet has the most moons?"
I froze. My mind went blank. I looked away from the quizmaster and tapped my pencil on the table.
Lalremsiami, our team captain, leaned in. "Take your time, Kavitha."
I remembered reading about it in a library book. Jupiter? Or was it Saturn? I thought about the picture of Saturn's rings, with little dots around them.
"Saturn," I said finally.
"Correct!" said the quizmaster.
Lalremsiami grinned. Later she said, "You looked so serious. I knew you were thinking."

qa.q: What did Kavitha tap on the table?
qa.a: A pencil.

qa.q: What was Kavitha feeling when the mind went blank?
qa.a: Kavitha felt nervous and under pressure, but kept thinking instead of giving up.

qa.q: What did Lalremsiami do that helped?
qa.a: She told Kavitha to take time, giving space to think instead of rushing.

qa.q: How might Lalremsiami have seen Kavitha's silence?
qa.a: She saw it as serious thinking and trusted Kavitha to find the answer.

grounding: The narrator recalls needing silence and time to think during a quiz, and a teammate waiting.

passage:
Teacher's note, Class 5, maths hour
Today I asked the class how many different ways we could make 10 using only odd numbers. Avni's hand shot up at once. Harsha went quiet, looked out of the window and tapped a pencil against his chin. In the past I would have moved on, thinking Harsha was lost. This time I said, "Let's give everyone ten more seconds." I counted in my head. At about eight, Harsha turned back and said, "You can never do it with three odd numbers, because three odd numbers always make an odd number." That was exactly the idea I had hoped someone would find. Next step: I will keep a waiting pause after every big question, and tell the class why.

qa.q: What maths question did the teacher ask?
qa.a: How many different ways they could make 10 using only odd numbers.

qa.q: What might Harsha have been feeling and thinking while he looked out of the window?
qa.a: He was thinking hard and curious about a pattern, not lost or bored, as his answer showed.

qa.q: What did the teacher change, and why did it help?
qa.a: The teacher waited ten extra seconds instead of moving on, which let Harsha finish thinking and share the key idea.

qa.q: How might Avni see the extra ten seconds?
qa.a: Avni, whose hand went up first, might feel impatient, but also gets to hear a deeper idea she might not have reached.

grounding: It illustrates a child's silence, looking away and chin-tapping as signs of thinking, and a teacher's extra wait letting the child finish.
